_note: Short, speakable facts for common US birds. Entries marked verified were checked against published sources; the rest are drafted from general knowledge and should be spot-checked (All About Birds, Birds of the World) before you rely on them. Keys match BirdNET labels by scientific name first, then common name. Add a bird by appending an entry; keep look_tip and fun_fact to one short sentence each.

species.habitat: lawns, parks, woodland edges and suburban yards
species.look_tip: Look on open lawns, or high on a treetop perch when it sings.
species.fun_fact: It is often among the first birds to sing before dawn.

species.habitat: thickets, forest edges, gardens and parks
species.look_tip: Look low in dense shrubs, or high on a perch when it sings.
species.fun_fact: Unusually for songbirds, females sing as well as males.

species.habitat: oak and mixed woodland, suburbs and city parks
species.look_tip: Look in the upper branches of oaks and other tall trees.
species.fun_fact: It sometimes imitates the calls of hawks.

species.habitat: fields, woodland edges, towns and cities
species.look_tip: Look on open ground, or on high branches and wires.
species.fun_fact: Family groups stay together, with older young helping to raise new chicks.

species.habitat: brushy edges, marshes, hedgerows and gardens
species.look_tip: Look for a small streaky bird singing from a low perch in shrubs.
species.fun_fact: Each male sings several different song types.

species.habitat: open country, farmland, suburbs and parks
species.look_tip: Look on wires, fence posts and open ground.
species.fun_fact: Its wings make a whistling sound when it takes off.

species.habitat: deciduous and mixed woods, thickets and feeders
species.look_tip: Look for small flocks flitting through branches at eye level.
species.fun_fact: Extra dee notes at the end of its call can signal a more dangerous predator nearby.

species.habitat: woods, thickets and backyards in the Southeast
species.look_tip: Look for small flocks flitting through branches at eye level.
species.fun_fact: Its song has four notes, where the Black-capped Chickadee's has two.

species.habitat: deciduous woods, parks and backyards
species.look_tip: Look in the mid-level branches of oaks and other broadleaf trees.
species.fun_fact: It sometimes lines its nest with hair plucked from living animals.

species.habitat: woodlands, orchards, parks and backyards
species.look_tip: Look for it clinging to trunks, thin branches and weed stalks.
species.fun_fact: It is the smallest woodpecker in North America.

species.habitat: mature deciduous and mixed woods
species.look_tip: Look for it creeping headfirst down tree trunks.
species.fun_fact: It wedges large seeds into bark and hacks them open with its bill.

species.habitat: dense tangles, brush piles and wooded edges
species.look_tip: Look low in tangles and brush, often with its tail cocked up.
species.fun_fact: Its loud, ringing song carries far for such a small bird.

species.habitat: towns, suburbs, farms and open woodland
species.look_tip: Look on wires, feeders and treetops.
species.fun_fact: The male's red color comes from pigments in the food it eats.

species.habitat: conifer and mixed woods, plus winter fields and yards
species.look_tip: Look for it hopping on the ground near cover.
species.fun_fact: White outer tail feathers flash as it flies away.

species.habitat: marshes, wet meadows and roadside ditches
species.look_tip: Look for males singing from the tops of cattails and reeds.
species.fun_fact: Males flash red shoulder patches to defend their territory.

species.habitat: marsh edges, wet meadows and thick low vegetation
species.look_tip: Look low in dense reeds and shrubs; males sing from open stems.
species.fun_fact: Its song is often written as witchety-witchety-witchety.

species.habitat: streamsides, bridges, barns and open woods
species.look_tip: Look for it perched low near water, wagging its tail.
species.fun_fact: In 1804 it became the first bird banded in North America, by Audubon.

species.habitat: shrubby edges, thickets and brushy woodland
species.look_tip: Look for it scratching in leaf litter beneath thick shrubs.
species.fun_fact: It kicks both feet backward at once to uncover food.

species.habitat: shady, moist deciduous forest
species.look_tip: Look on the forest floor and low branches in shady woods.
species.fun_fact: It can sing two notes at once.

species.habitat: mature deciduous and mixed forest
species.look_tip: Look for it walking on the leafy forest floor.
species.fun_fact: Its dome-shaped ground nest looks like a small outdoor oven.

species.habitat: deciduous forest canopy
species.look_tip: Look high in the leafy canopy; it is far easier to hear than to see.
species.fun_fact: A male may sing thousands of times in a single day.

species.habitat: dense thickets, shrubby edges and gardens
species.look_tip: Look low in thick shrubs and tangles.
species.fun_fact: Its mewing call sounds like a cat.

species.habitat: open suburbs, parks and shrubby fields
species.look_tip: Look on rooftops, wires and shrub tops.
species.fun_fact: Some males sing through the night, imitating other birds.

species.habitat: cities, towns and farms
species.look_tip: Look around buildings, hedges and feeders.
species.fun_fact: It was introduced to North America in the 1850s.

species.habitat: cities, suburbs, farms and open ground
species.look_tip: Look on lawns, wires and rooftops.
species.fun_fact: It was introduced to New York City in 1890 and spread across the continent.

species.habitat: mature wet woods and swampy forest
species.look_tip: Look at dusk for a large round-headed owl on a big branch near the trunk.
species.fun_fact: Its call is often written as who cooks for you.

species.habitat: woodlands, farmland, deserts and city parks
species.look_tip: Look for a large owl with ear tufts, perched against a trunk at dusk.
species.fun_fact: It often nests in late winter, using old nests built by other birds.

species.habitat: open woods, edges, lawns and parks
species.look_tip: Look on the ground in lawns, or clinging to trunks.
species.fun_fact: It often feeds on the ground, eating ants.

species.habitat: weedy fields, roadsides and gardens
species.look_tip: Look on the seed heads of thistles and other weeds.
species.fun_fact: It nests late in summer, when thistle seed is plentiful.

species.habitat: open country with scattered trees, farms and orchards
species.look_tip: Look on fence posts, wires and low branches over open ground.
species.fun_fact: It nests in tree cavities and readily uses nest boxes.

species.habitat: mature deciduous and mixed woods
species.look_tip: Look on a bare mid-level branch, from where it darts out after insects.
species.fun_fact: It keeps singing at dusk, after most other birds have stopped.

species.habitat: lawns, parks, open woods and conifer edges
species.look_tip: Look on short grass and low conifer branches.
species.fun_fact: Its song is a long, dry trill on a single pitch.

species.habitat: mature woods, suburbs and parks
species.look_tip: Look on trunks and large limbs.
species.fun_fact: Its red belly blush is faint and rarely seen.
